name: Opus 5 unrestricted
strategy: Concentrated bet on the 2026 oil-supply-shock rotation: ~53% effective energy exposure via 2x ERX plus refiner MPC, carried by low-correlation healthcare/financials/defense longs, hedged by a short in oil-taxed consumer discretionary and a small stopped short-DOGE perp, with 8% cash at 4%.

positions.thesis: Raised 12 to 20 and now my largest position, because this is the only leg in the book that got a live proof rather than an argument this week: MPC closed at an all-time high $367.99 on 8/28 during a week Brent fell more than 5%. That is the exact divergence I sized it for. Refining margin is a product-scarcity bet, not a crude-price bet, and the scarcity is at records with a physical basis I can point at — the US diesel crack hit $102.20/bbl on 8/17, the first triple-digit print in history and ~15% above the 2022 record, and still sits near $93-94; roughly 7-8 mb/d of global refining capacity is offline from Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries and Gulf drone damage; and US distillate inventories are at their lowest since 1996. Against that, falling crude is a tailwind: the refiner buys the cheaper feedstock and sells into a market that is still physically short distillate. MPC's own refining and marketing margin has gone $17.58 to $36.33 per barrel — realized cash, not a forecast. I am buying more at an all-time high, which is the honest cost of a setup that is working; the real risk is that record cracks mean-revert as offline capacity returns or demand rectifies, and heading into winter with 30-year-low distillate stocks that reversion looks like a Q1 problem rather than a September one. Stop -18% caps the leg at 3.6% of NAV. Take-profit cut 40 to 35 because at that level the crack has to have held records for a full quarter, and I would rather be paid on a mean-reverting spread than greedy.

Held at 20, and its job just got more important. This was ballast for a 2x energy fund; it is now ballast for a book whose largest exposures are a single-factor bet on refined-product scarcity, held into a Fed chair who has openly put rate hikes back on the table with the S&P at 7,711 and records. Healthcare at ~18x forward with a 0.65-0.75 beta, carried by real Q2 earnings beats and the GLP-1 franchise rather than by defensive flows, is the cleanest thing I own for a multiple-compression regime — when the discount rate rises, the low-multiple low-beta sector gives back least. It stays unstopped for the same reason as last week, unchanged: this is the position I want to still be holding if everything else here is wrong, and a stop on my lowest-beta leg would only fire in a market-wide flush, which is precisely the moment I need to be holding it. Its honest weakness is that it did nothing at all this week (~$172.4), and in a book that just cut both of its exciting theses, that is a feature.

Trimmed 20 to 14 because the reason I wrote for owning 20 is no longer true. I sized this on 'Powell opening the door to a September cut with markets at 91% odds'; Warsh told Jackson Hole that underlying inflation trends have not meaningfully improved and the Fed has more work to do, the two-year went 4.22 to 4.30, and September hike odds are near 50%. Rising real rates are the single cleanest headwind to a non-yielding asset and I will not pretend otherwise to protect a position. I trim rather than exit because the rest of the bid is intact and demonstrated itself under fire this week: gold made $4,697 on 8/25 and still closed 8/28 at $4,608 immediately after an explicitly hawkish speech, with central banks buying a quarterly record 288.9 tonnes in Q2 against $40 trillion of federal debt. And a Fed hiking into a labor market that shed 23,000 jobs is a stagflationary policy-error setup, which is the one regime where gold works with rates going the wrong way. Stop held at -12%, capping the leg at 1.7% of NAV; a 12% break from a record would mean the fiscal and central-bank bid failed too, and at that point I am wrong on all of it rather than early.

New 10%, and the reason it is a second name rather than simply a larger MPC is idiosyncratic risk. The dominant single-name event for a refiner is an unplanned outage — a fire, a unit trip, a turnaround overrun — and in a market this tight, one of those at one facility is company-specific pain while the sector thesis stays perfectly intact. Splitting 30% of crack exposure across two operators converts a plant-level accident from a 5-6% NAV event into roughly half that. Valero is the purest expression of the trade: the least diversified of the large US refiners away from refining itself, so the most levered to the distillate crack that is actually at records, with a Gulf Coast system positioned into cheapening feedstock as crude falls. Same thesis, same catalyst and the same failure mode as MPC — record cracks mean-reverting when the ~7-8 mb/d of offline global capacity returns — which is why the pair together is 30 and not 45. I could not pull a fresh 8/28 quote before my research budget ran out, so I am sizing this at 10 rather than 15 and putting the same -18% stop on it, capping the leg at 1.8% of NAV.

Held at 10, and I want to correct the lazy bear case against it: crude falling 5% does NOT relieve airlines, because carriers buy the refined product, not the barrel, and the jet-fuel crack sits inside the same record complex I just increased my long exposure to. That is the point of the pair — MPC and VLO are long the crack, JETS short is short the crack's largest captive consumer, and both legs pay off on the same physical fact of refined-product scarcity. The industry has already conceded the math: the global sector nearly halved its 2026 profit forecast on Middle East fuel costs, US carriers' fuel bill ran $6.66bn in May at +85% y/y, roughly 20% of exported jet fuel is still stranded, and managements are cutting unprofitable routes and grounding less fuel-efficient aircraft. The demand leg strengthened independently this week: a Fed chair signaling hikes into a soft labor market pressures discretionary leisure travel, which flinches first when fares rise to cover fuel. What improved is that this no longer double-counts with a large crude long — cutting ERX removed the shared Hormuz failure mode I flagged last week, so this is a cleaner hedge than it was. Squeeze risk stays specific: the $2.5bn Frontier/Avelo federal liquidity ask with a possible government equity stake. Borrow costs ~30bps a year on 10%. Stop -18% caps it at 1.8% of NAV; take-profit held at +25%.

Cut 22 to 8 — the largest single change in the book and an admission that I was long the wrong end of the energy complex. I bought this on supply removal. Supply is coming back: Persian Gulf exports have recovered from a March low of 5-6 mb/d to 15-16 mb/d, the 8/24 sanctions package landed softer than its 'toughest in history' billing and oil fell on the news, and on 8/26 Iran and Oman announced a phased framework for a temporary 7-mile Hormuz corridor with joint mine-clearing. Brent went $93.86 to ~$88.5 and XLE $63.58 to $62.50. The market has reclassified this from a physical-supply threat to an economic confrontation, and a 2x fund with daily-reset decay is an expensive way to be stubborn about a thesis that has moved from base case to tail. Layer on a Fed that may hike: a firmer dollar and slower demand are both crude-negative. Why 8 and not zero — the re-escalation tail is genuinely live, not rhetorical. The June interim deal has lapsed, Iran publicly says the US is blocking the Hormuz agreement, the corridor is explicitly temporary and conditional on US compliance, mines are still in the water, and roughly 8 mb/d is still missing from the market. If that unravels, crude gaps up hard and 2x is the cheapest way to have owned the option. At 8% with a stop tightened -22% to -20% the leg costs at most 1.6% of NAV, a price I will pay rather than be flat a live geopolitical binary. Take-profit held at +40%.

Cut 10 to 5, the sharpest proportional trim in the book, because this is the leg whose written thesis was most explicitly a rate-cut bet — I raised it from 7 to 10 only last week citing 'a September cut at 91% implied odds.' Those odds are now roughly a coin flip on a HIKE. Silver is the higher-beta expression of the debasement trade, which means it is the higher-beta expression of a driver that just inverted, and its industrial half is precisely what a Fed deliberately slowing the economy damages — so both legs I bought it for weakened at once. It went flat on the week ($69.87 to $69.35) after an 8.8% run, so the gold/silver catch-up I paid up for has stalled rather than continued. I keep 5 rather than none because the structural supply deficit is independent of the Fed, silver is still well below its February mid-$80s high while gold sits near a record, and if the policy-error stagflation path is what Warsh is actually engineering then silver leads gold on the way up. But it is now a tail position, not a thesis position. Stop stays wide at -18%, capping it at 0.9% of NAV; this metal traded mid-$80s to $64 to $70 inside a year and anything tighter is noise.

reassessment_note: Weekly desk 2026-08-29: Two of my three stated premises broke this week and I am not going to hold positions whose written reasons are now false. The ERX thesis was supply removal — blockade plus 'toughest sanctions in history.' The sanctions landed softer than billed, Iran and Oman announced a phased Hormuz corridor framework with joint mine-clearing, Gulf exports have recovered from 5-6 mb/d in March to 15-16 mb/d, and Brent fell 5%+ to ~$88.5. That is my named worst tail arriving in slow motion rather than as a gap, which is the version where I actually get to act on it. The GLD and SLV sizes were justified in writing by '91% odds of a September cut'; Warsh used his first Jackson Hole speech to put rate HIKES in play, the two-year moved to 4.30%, and September hike odds are near 50%. Meanwhile the one leg that does not depend on either premise got materially stronger: the diesel crack printed a record $102.20, sits near $93-94, distillate inventories are at a 30-year low, 7-8 mb/d of refining capacity is offline, and MPC made an all-time high in the same week crude fell 5%. Cheaper crude is a feedstock tailwind to the crack, not a headwind. So I am selling the barrel and buying the bottleneck: ERX 22 to 8, MPC 12 to 20, new VLO 10, and the book's center of gravity moves from 'crude goes up' to 'refined products stay scarce' — a thesis that survives the de-escalation that is killing the old one and is paired against a short in the product's captive consumer. Metals go 30 to 19 because their engine reversed, not to zero, because gold held $4,608 through an explicitly hawkish Jackson Hole on record central-bank buying. Cash to 13 because a Fed that may hike makes 4%+ a real competing asset, and because I just cut my highest-conviction directional bet and do not want to force the proceeds somewhere to avoid looking idle.
novelty: I manage only a Round-3 book, so there is no Round-2 book to overlap with; the novelty is structural rather than nominal — this is no longer a levered crude bet carried by hedges but a long-crack-spread book, expressed as long two refiners and short the refined product's largest captive consumer, with the crude leg demoted to a small option on re-escalation.
research_notes:
Two regime breaks this week, both against my stated theses, and one confirmation.

1) CRUDE — my ERX thesis broke. Brent fell from $93.86 to ~$88.3-89.3, a >5% weekly loss and the first weekly decline in three. The mechanism matters more than the price: (a) the Bessent "economic D-Day" sanctions that I explicitly bought last week landed Monday 8/24 and were, per market analysts, LESS severe than anticipated — oil fell on the announcement; (b) Iran and Oman announced a phased framework on 8/26 for a temporary 7-mile-wide Hormuz transit corridor plus a joint mine-clearing initiative, with Oman "hopeful" of formalizing; (c) Goldman puts Persian Gulf exports back at ~15-16 mb/d versus a March low of 5-6 mb/d (pre-conflict 22-24). Traders have reclassified this from a physical-supply threat to a sanctions/economic confrontation. That is not a headline gap-down — it is the slow version of exactly the tail I named as my largest risk. XLE $63.58 -> $62.50. Offsetting: the interim peace deal has lapsed, Iran says the US is blocking the Hormuz deal, mines are still in the water, and ~8 mb/d is still missing. Re-escalation is live but no longer the base case.

2) THE FED — inverted. Kevin Warsh gave his first Jackson Hole speech on 8/28 and said inflation reports "do not tell me that underlying trends have meaningfully improved," that the Fed "has more work to do," and put rate INCREASES in play. Two-year yield 4.22% -> 4.30%; CME FedWatch September hike odds moved to roughly 50%; consensus commentary is no hike in September but one by October or December. My GLD and SLV theses were written verbatim around "Powell opening the door to a September cut with markets at 91% odds." That premise is gone. Notably, gold barely flinched — spot $4,608 on 8/28 after a $4,697 high on 8/25, with central banks buying a quarterly record 288.9 tonnes in Q2 — so the non-rate bid (fiscal, central banks, geopolitics) is real, but the specific reason I was 30% in metals is not. Silver $69.35, flat on the week after last week's 8.8% run.

3) REFINING — confirmed, and confirmed in the best possible way. The US diesel crack hit a record $102.20/bbl on 8/17 (first triple-digit print ever, ~15% above the Oct-2022 record) and sits near $93-94 in late August; NWE gasoil crack ~$78, Singapore ~$72; roughly 7-8 mb/d of global refining capacity is offline from Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries and Gulf drone attacks; US distillate inventories entering late August are at their lowest since 1996, a 30-year trough. MPC printed an all-time high of $367.99 on 8/28 — an all-time high in the same week crude fell 5%. That is the divergence I bought MPC for, demonstrated in live fire rather than argued.

4) EQUITIES/AIRLINES — S&P 7,711.76, +0.49% on the week, Nasdaq +0.9%, index at records into a hawkish Fed. XLV ~$172.4, still the low-beta ballast, unremarkable week. On JETS: lower crude does NOT relieve airlines while the crack is at a record, because carriers buy the product, not the barrel — jet fuel is inside the same squeeze complex. IATA still has the industry's 2026 profit forecast roughly halved, US carrier fuel spend ran $6.66bn in May at +85% y/y, and ~20% of exported jet fuel is still stranded. A Fed threatening hikes into a soft labor market strengthens the demand-side leg independently.

Synthesis: the correct read is that I was long the wrong end of the energy complex. The crude bet depended on supply staying removed; supply is coming back. The crack bet depends on refining capacity staying destroyed and distillate inventories staying empty — and cheaper crude is a direct feedstock tailwind to it. I am rotating from the barrel to the barrel's bottleneck, and cutting the metals sizing that was justified by a rate cut that is now a coin-flip rate hike. Note: my web-research budget ran out before I could pull a fresh 8/28 quote on VLO, which is reflected in that position being sized at 10 rather than larger.
